title: Competitive Sports
summary:
Pregnancy does not require stopping sport, but competitive athletes face extreme physiological, metabolic, and psychological demands that need case-by-case medical, biomechanical, and psychological review. Whether an athlete can continue depends on prior training level, the type of sport, the trimester, and the obstetric condition, with coordination among gynecologists, physiotherapists, and trainers.

The chapter sorts sports into generally safe, moderate risk, and contraindicated groups, describes adaptations for each trimester, and gives advice for athletics, swimming, cycling, team sports, and strength sports. It closes with a phased postpartum return plan and a call for clubs and federations to provide flexibility and support.
points: Sports are grouped as generally safe (for example swimming, stationary cycling, light jogging), moderate risk, or contraindicated.
Moderate-risk sports include competitive running, triathlon, road cycling, team contact sports, combat sports, and high-intensity strength training such as CrossFit or weightlifting.
Combat sports are contraindicated in competition, though non-contact technical training is possible in the first trimester.
Contraindicated sports include diving, motorsports, equestrian, climbing, skydiving, paragliding, aggressive alpine skiing, surfing, and mountain biking.
The first trimester (0-12 weeks) calls for moderate volume, avoiding overheating, and watching for nausea, fatigue, or dizziness.
The second trimester (13-27 weeks) allows near-normal training with postural adjustments and no prolonged supine exercise.
The third trimester (28-40 weeks) calls for lower intensity, no impact, and a focus on stabilizing strength and pelvic control.
Strength athletes should stay preferably below 70% of 1RM and avoid the Valsalva maneuver.

Postpartum return runs in phases: 0-6 weeks recovery and pelvic floor, 6-12 weeks light aerobic and basic strength, 3-6 months progressive sport-specific load, and no high-intensity competition before 6 months.
takeaways: Plan training with your gynecologist, physiotherapist, and trainer.
Swap sprints and plyometrics for controlled lower-intensity intervals.
Favor stationary bikes or rollers over outdoor riding.
In contact team sports, suspend competition and keep non-contact technical sessions.
Prioritize technique, breathing, and pelvic control as pregnancy advances.
Return gradually after birth, with an obstetric evaluation and pelvic floor rehabilitation first.
cautions: Suspend competition in contact team sports during pregnancy.
Avoid deep diving in swimming because of pressure and fetal oxygenation risks.
Monitor the placenta, cervix, blood pressure, and blood glucose in athletes who continue.
